Adding a small amount of baking soda to the cooking liquid seems to help the beans soften up by counteracting the acidic tomatoes.

I prefer this with one can of roasted tomatoes instead of two. Two cans make it unpleasantly sweet to me.

One or two canned chipotles en adobo, plus some of the liquid from the cans, are a welcome addition.

You can do them without epazote and they are passable but the epazote adds something which isn't an obvious taste on its own but accentuates the other flavors. [It also supposedly lowers the methane production according to folk tales]. Don't overdo the chiles since this is not supposed to be a super spicy dish. I also would not use as many tomatoes as this recipe calls for - the tomatoes should just tint the broth, not color it or have a discernable tomato flavor. I have only had these beans made with salt pork so I am looking at that bacon with concern.

These beans and some corn tortillas will give you the essential proteins and carbohydrates one needs to live but the dish is typically a side dish served with other items as well. We do taco night with the neighbors once a month here in Puerto Vallarta and these beans are always served along with the carne asada, fresh tortillas, assorted salsas, guac, and salad stuff - pickled and fresh.

I know how everyone will always take a recipe and alter it to make it their own. That's great to do and I have certain little alterations I make on the beans myself. But whenever possible I use my olla and a bed of coals to make them because there is no pressure cookers, slow cooker, or other device that can do justice to these beans. Sounds promising!\n\nAs to the origin story, I also think the brothel story is fanciful and apocryphal. Based on my research, here's the real deal: It probably evolved from a classic marinara sauce when someone figured out that olives and capers were a nice addition to a tomato and garlic sauce. (Apparently, the anchovies only came later.) Older Neapolitan cookbooks even have early versions of a tomato, olive, and caper sauce that they call 'alla marinara'! Another name is 'con aulive e cchiapparielle', that is, 'with olives and capers' in the Neapolitan dialect, and that name is apparently still in use in the Naples area. The name 'puttanesca', literally meaning 'whorish', was probably first applied in the 1950s. (The first appearance of the name in print is in a 1958 cookbook called \"With Gusto and Relish\", written by a couple English and American expatriates living in Rome.) The origin of the name and the modern version of the sauce was on the fashionable vacation island of Ischia (near Naples) and was originally 'alla puttana', puttana meaning literally 'whorish', but the actual meaning is bullshitty, crappy, foolish, nonsensical, flashy, etc. The idea being that the sauce is made with mostly canned ingredients, so basically, any old crap you have lying around the kitchen, as well as the flashy color contrast of the completed sauce. Since 'puttanata' is considered slightly vulgar in Italian, it was altered to the apparently somewhat less-vulgar 'puttanesca'. The Naples brothel backstory was probably invented after the fact. There's a pretty good account of its history here: https://www.gamberorossointernational.com/news/the-history-of-spaghetti-alla-puttanesca-and-where-to-eat-it-in-naples/\n \nSome comments on the recipe, as someone who's made a lot of puttanesca sauce over the years. (It being one of my go-to recipes, and one I make in large batches, which I freeze some of in small containers so I always have some handy for when I don't feel like cooking from scratch.)\n\nMy biggest difference with your recipe - why do you cook the olives and capers in hot oil???? This is totally unnecessary, and if anything, cooks off some of their flavor. These should be chopped up and mixed, put aside, and added in at the very end (along with fresh herbs) after the tomato sauce has thickened. Believe me, the flavors still merge and your olives and capers will be in much better shape.\n\nGarlic: I agree with you about how long cooking of the garlic in oil develops good flavor. Beside being careful with your temperature, here's another trick: add water to your garlic while you're chopping it up. Use a fair amount, up to a teaspoon, as much as the crushed garlic will hold. This allows you to lengthen the sauteing time of the garlic considerably and really gives you a wonderful garlic flavor in the end.\n\nChili pepper: Yes, I know Italian pepper flakes are 'traditional', but Vietnamese-style chili-garlic sauce works much better (it's a go-to in my fridge) or even a fresh hot chili pepper minced up.\n\nOlives: Gaeta olives are the 'canonical' one, coming from more or less the same part of Italy where puttanesca sauce originated, but they can be very hard to find. I use Nicoise olives, which are very similar. I only use Kalamata when I can't find the other kinds. Good olives really makes a difference. Also - no need to pit the olives one at a time with a kitchen knife! Put your olives in a folded clean towel, then take a broad kitchen mallet and give it some good whacks, then roll the olives around while still in the towel. Pitting by hand, perhaps with the aid of a small paring knife, wil be easy. Then a quick course chop of the olives and capers (the latter may not even need chopping). Be sure to rinse the brine off before using - olives and capers actually have a nicer flavor this way.\n\nTomatoes: Good quality canned ones, obviously, and there are really good ones from both Italy and the USA. But during summer, I go half-and-half with canned tomatoes and the nicest heirloom tomatoes I can find at the local farmers market. I most recently used Cherokee Purple tomatoes, and the result was the best sauce I'd ever made! I do this in two steps - I add the canned ones first along with some reserved puree from the can, and cook that down into a fairly thick sauce. Then add the coarsely diced fresh tomatoes (and any juice that's come out of them) without mixing them at first. I turn the heat down and let the fresh tomatoes slowly cook on top of the layer of the other sauce. When the chunks of tomato are cooked but not broken down, I mix them in and then do the finishing steps on the sauce. You get some incredible tomato flavor this way. Also, I don't use all or even most of the tomato puree in the can - I add a little (about 1/4 cup or so per can) when I'm making the sauce itself, then I add some more back when I'm putting together the prepared sauce and noodles, but otherwise, don't use most of the puree and end up freezing it for other uses.\n\nOther additions: a little but of tomato paste (from a tube) sauteed along with the anchovies at the beginning for even more tomato flavor. Lemon juice and lemon zest along with the herbs at the end to brighten the flavor up. Herbs can vary - basil, parsley, or oregano all work well - use what's available, fresh, and seasonal. Be super-careful about adding salt, since so many of the ingredients are salty - if I add any, it's at the end when I'm adjusting the seasoning. Be careful about how much chili you add at the beginning, since black pepper will also add to the spiciness. This is something that can be adjusted at the final seasoning step.\n\nCheese: Although it's not necessary with a good sauce, it's a nice addition. I highly recommend pecorino sardo if you can find it!\n\nOptional fish to add to the final dish: I agree with you, a good Italian-style canned tuna is a nice addition. I've also gotten wonderful results from canned octopus. (Albeit, I'm have qualms about eating octopus now, as there's increasing evidence that these are quite intelligent creatures, on par with primates.)   "recipeInstructions": [
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 1,
      "name": null,
      "text": "In a medium saucepan of boiling salted water, cook penne until just short of al dente, about 1 minute less than the package recommends.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Meanwhile, in a large skillet, combine oil, garlic, and pepper flakes. Cook over medium heat until garlic is very lightly golden, about 5 minutes. (Adjust heat as necessary to keep it gently sizzling.)",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/rj2q_nv69zqfuYf5RX8TsEt8xmM=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__images__2016__02__20160211-pasta-arrabiata-vicky-wasik-001-91dc57bd9151441c8dea1e976de54ca2.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add tomatoes, stir to combine, and bring to a bare simmer. When pasta is ready, transfer it to sauce using a strainer or slotted spoon. (Alternatively, drain pasta through a colander, reserving 1 cup of cooking water. Add drained pasta to sauce.)",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/mRh9fpxuE5lQnfeWbntgplg9FMk=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__images__2016__02__20160211-pasta-arrabiata-vicky-wasik-002-433c059de5604b7a9b1a68d266edda65.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add about 1/4 cup pasta water to sauce and increase heat to bring pasta and sauce to a vigorous simmer. Cook, stirring and shaking the pan and adding more pasta water as necessary to keep sauce loose, until pasta is perfectly al dente, 1 to 2 minutes longer. (The pasta will cook more slowly in the sauce than it did in the water.)",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/PJ7mpfIC5i_3go5c39L4OL5wihA=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__images__2016__02__20160211-pasta-arrabiata-collage-vicky-wasik-011-679690c9d5f54020902189a51e1fe54f.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {

      "position": 5,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Continue cooking pasta until sauce thickens and begins to coat noodles, then remove from heat and toss in cheese and parsley, stirring vigorously to incorporate.       },
      "reviewBody": "10x as much garlic goes into an arrabiatta. A couple anchovies or a teaspoon of fish sauce adds a nice level. And use fresh peppers if you have.",

        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Adam"
      },
      "reviewBody": "I like to use the jarred chopped Calabrian chilis for arrabiata. I use about a tablespoon for moderate heat. I like the bite and acidity that they add.",
      "datePublished": "2022-02-26T19:09:39.000Z"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Binko"
      },
      "reviewBody": "@ thesteveroller: I know I'm about three years too late, but saying its \"Solancae Capsicum annum L\" means very little in terms of determining the exact chile and its heat level. That descriptions covers everything from sweet paprika to cayenne to Thai birds' eye chiles.Here in the US, it is usually a blend of peppers, typically cayenne, New Mexico, California peppers, etc. The aim is for a product of about 30K Scoville. More here: https://www.thedailymeal.co...",
      "datePublished": "2019-01-13T18:07:28.000Z"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",

      },
      "reviewBody": "Most diced tomatoes are made from about the worst tomatoes companies are allowed to sell.",

    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "drtcn"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Absolutely perfect with a full tablespoon of pepper, surprisingly awesome flavor. Wouldn't change a thing to the recipe.",

    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "thesteveroller"
      },
      "reviewBody": "@All-a-Mort, or Daniel could have simply answered that in the US when you say crushed red pepper flakes, the understanding, unless one is being really obtuse, is something like these: http://www.mccormick.com/Sp...They are \"The dehydrated, crushed flakes of the annual, Solanaceae Capsicum annum L.\" We even get little packets of them when we order take out pizza. Now, isn't that a clearer answer?",
      "datePublished": "2016-03-03T13:51:00.000Z"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "elangomatt"
      },
      "reviewBody": "@J.R. Stevens You can probably use diced tomatoes instead of whole tomatoes but the sauce will probably end up chunkier. Diced tomatoes generally have calcium chloride added which keeps them intact longer during cooking. Whole tomatoes don't have that calcium chloride as often I think so the break down faster when cooked.",
      "datePublished": "2016-02-29T21:04:58.000Z"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Daniel Gritzer"
      },
      "reviewBody": "@All-a-Mort Your question highlights how futile it is to give measurements for red pepper flakes. @Liam wrote above that Batali uses 1 tablespoon for a pound of dried pasta, but some chili flakes, if used in that quantity, would render the dish inedible...maybe even dangerous. Other types might be so mild that a full tablespoon still wouldn't be enough to make the dish truly spicy (though those are probably not the kind you'd want to use here). In Italy, red chili flakes are made from peperoncini (plural), but that's a generic word for small hot red chilies and so still doesn't get you an answer. Most of the hot chilies I've had in Italy have been medium to midium-high heat, just based on my own tolerance, but that doesn't mean none of them are atomic...some surely are. There's no easy answer...there are many cultivars of spicy red chilies that span a wide heat range, all of which can be dried and crumbled into flakes. The key is to know how hot the dried chili flakes are that you have, and add according to your own taste. Getting more specific than that is incredibly difficult.",
      "datePublished": "2016-02-29T19:54:57.000Z"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "All-a-Mort"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Out of curiosity, what exactly constitutes 'crushed red pepper' or 'red pepper flakes' in the US (I'm assuming these are the same thing?) I often see it listed in recipes (and news reports of the activities of scampish school children in Florida) but am at a loss to find a point of comparison.In the UK, crushed red chillies could be anything from mild pseudo-kashmiri (real Kashmir grown chillies are not exported so I am informed) and unnamed dried red chilli flakes (probably a type jalape\u00f1o or cayenne) to Thai prik kee noo, of which a scant 1/4 teaspoon is easily sufficient to make a sauce angry (any more and you risk making your diners angry).",
      "datePublished": "2016-02-29T19:46:20.000Z"
    }
  ],

  "recipeInstructions": [
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 1,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Fill a large bowl with cold water and stir in enough salt to make it salty like the sea (a 3% salt solution, by weight, is a good ratio). Add clams and let stand for 30 minutes. Lift clams from bowl and discard sandy water. Rinse out bowl and repeat this purging process until clams no longer release sand into the water (usually 2 to 3 purging cycles). Discard any clams that are gaping open and refuse to close when tapped. Set clean clams aside.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/eqfU7uXHknT4LSwYeVKCSZ8s8O0=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-29f40f46816f4d3398987b2d7292d153.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Heat 3 tablespoons (45ml) oil in a deep 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add shallots, season lightly with salt, and cook, stirring occasionally, until shallots start to soften, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 30 seconds.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/KmQ2GtkdNvnmt4HDTVdizPYj0XE=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-step2-835164484c7548dc9d3b2dd05ab7b850.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add wine and clams, increase heat to high, cover, and cook, shaking pan frequently, for 4 minutes. Uncover and, using tongs, transfer any clams that have opened to a medium bowl; cover bowl with foil to keep warm. Add mussels to skillet, cover, and continue to cook, shaking pan frequently and uncovering to stir and check shellfish every 45 seconds, until clams and mussels have all opened, 3 to 4 minutes longer. Using tongs, quickly transfer shellfish to bowl, and cover; leave aromatics and liquid in pan. Discard any clams or mussels that do not open.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/OI-2wpuK-dlofN2vIg7_5h1XePw=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-step3-1-bbd0d51a5fd848009020df19c0d85896.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add clam juice and 2 cups (475ml) water to skillet and bring mixture to a boil over high heat. Add spaghetti and cook, stirring constantly for the first 30 seconds to prevent noodles from sticking and then stirring occasionally, until pasta begins to have some flexibility and is softened on the exterior, but well shy of al dente and still uncooked in the center, about 3 minutes less than the package directions. Add water in 1/4 cup (60ml) increments as needed to ensure pasta cooks evenly and doesn't stick to the bottom of the pan.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/4VuX5vfNvpT4t4PndPfmmNssREM=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-9-c88017d423164990961f55948dae2245.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 5,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Meanwhile, pull meat from about half of the clam shells and half of the mussel shells; discard empty shells and return shucked clams and mussels to bowl with remaining shell-on shellfish. Cover to keep warm.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/5hcOMn9GBD91TVpEYjd2Y_dyF_Y=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-11-714f471e0aea4aa0be0ee738b111f4a5.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 6,
      "name": null,
      "text": "When pasta is just softened on the exterior, add shrimp and squid to skillet. Continue to cook over high, stirring and tossing, until shrimp and squid are just cooked through, 2 to 4 minutes.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/MXfvCUZd0QahI9CTGWx9t2OV-Ns=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-12-8f7e1eece6cc445c98cece3c85fe5f62.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 7,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add tomatoes and all of the mussels and clams, along with any accumulated juices, and continue to cook over high, stirring and tossing constantly, until all of the seafood is heated through, pasta is al dente, and sauce is creamy and coats the pasta, about 1 minute; add more water, 2 tablespoons (30ml) at a time, if sauce over-reduces and becomes dry or greasy. Remove from heat, add parsley and lemon juice, and toss rapidly to incorporate. Season with salt to taste.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/gM5gMY8FkmXa-r-STawOMRMj9pI=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-16-141452b027b8480abc462f32929ee1c2.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 8,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Transfer to a large serving bowl or divide between individual serving bowls, arranging shell-on mussels and clams on top of pasta. Drizzle with remaining 1 tablespoon (15ml) oil, and serve.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/_bpJyuF-1GWuK9BE7GuaIbVBTtU=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/__opt__aboutcom__coeus__resources__content_migration__serious_eats__seriouseats.com__2021__03__20210301-Spaghetti-Allo-Scoglio-Tim-Chin-19-6ac10f44a82d46bdb6d42ca5ac18ca26.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    }

        "name": "Merry"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Scrumptious!! Came across this while looking for a recipe that would use a bag of mixed seafood I had in the freezer. Since I was using what I had in the pantry, I substituted vegetable broth for clam juice and used a squid ink spaghetti. It turned out so well I want to try it the right way with fresh seafood.       "text": "Place dried porcinis in a bowl and cover with boiling water. Cover with plastic wrap, and let soak for 30 minutes. Drain the mushrooms well, reserving all soaking liquid, and roughly chop porcinis.",

      "text": "Preheat broiler on high. In a large bowl, toss porcinis, button mushrooms, thyme, garlic, olive oil, and salt and pepper.       "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Meanwhile, bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil.       "text": "One major recommendation here. You\u2019re gonna want to form your trofie on a wooden surface. I used a cutting board. You don\u2019t want to use a super smooth surface or else the dough will just slide all over the place and won\u2019t form the little spiral shape. And, the wood also gives the surface of the pasta a nice texture to grab onto the pesto. Take your dough ball and pull off a small chunk, about 1/2 tsp. Aim for smaller, not bigger, here. Place your dough at the bottom of the board and stating with the tips of your fingers firmly roll up, like you were rolling the dough into a tube. Once the dough is at the base of your palm, keep pressure on it, and pull back and down at a 45 degree angle on the board using the outside of your hand, until you\u2019ve rolled out the full length of the dough. You need to keep enough pressure against the board on the way down to create that spiral shape. It\u2019ll take a few times to get used to it, at least it did for me, but once you get going, it\u2019s a bit meditative. Just be patient and enjoy the process until you\u2019ve used up all your dough. Also, these don\u2019t need to be perfectly uniform. Just try and keep them smaller, they taste better that way, and try to keep them roughly the same size so they cook at the same rate.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": "use store bought pasta",
      "text": "And, if this is not at all remotely appealing to you, you can just boil some store bought pasta. It\u2019s not a big deal.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 5,
      "name": "Make Pesto",
      "text": "Next up the pesto part. You can do this in a blender, food processor, using an immersion blender, or in a pestle and mortal. Totally up to you. Combine your garlic and nuts, and process till your have a sandy texture. Next add in your basil and oil and process till smooth. Lastly add in as much grated cheese as you like, stir to combine. Check if you need any salt, maybe some lemon? Pepper? Whatever you think it needs.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 6,
      "name": "Boil Trofie",
      "text": "The last bit is just boiling your trofie in salted water, usually about 12 minutes or so, but keep checking since it all depends on how big they are. Drain your pasta well, and off the heat add in plenty of that delish pesto. Top with some addition basil if you like, more cheese and eat up!",

  "review": [
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "AAA"
      },
      "reviewBody": "My family always removed the meat as well even though we still call it \"Sunday Gravy\" - i do this a little differently - after browning the meat, prepare the sauce with all of the seasoning and herbs (except basil goes in at the end), two of which are not mentioned here so i'll keep that secret :) but we let it come back up to a simmer and then add the meat back in and stew as this recipe states. I never experience mealy sausages but I will try saving the sausages until later though after reading this! One thing I'll say that i learned early on is too much onion kills the tomato flavor of imported tomatoes. I use only half an onion for like 3 or 4 cans of DOP tomatoes. When I make fast sauce with no meat, i don't use onion at all."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "walterhanig"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Are the meats cut into two pieces or two inch chunks? Are tomatoes drained?"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "roxlet"
      },
      "reviewBody": "One element that is missing is pork braciole made from the shoulder. And no onions. My Neapolitan mother used only garlic in her sauce. I might make it Sunday!"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "chefdavidrusso"
      },
      "reviewBody": "In your other oven-cooked tomato sauces (Best Slow-Cooked Tomato, and Best Slow Cooked Bolognese), you've held back a portion of the tomatoes until the end. I've made them both and I think it's an inspired idea. Why not in this sauce?"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Azerule"
      },
      "reviewBody": "@rmarcus8 Haha actually...2000 years ago Italians were using fish sauce (garum)...just saying.\n\nDefinitely making this soon"
    }
  ],

      "position": 1,
      "name": null,
      "text": "In a large skillet, heat olive oil over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add guanciale and pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until lightly browned, about 5 minutes. Add wine and cook, scraping up any browned bits on bottom of pan, until nearly evaporated, about 3 minutes.",

      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add tomatoes and bring to a simmer. Season with salt and pepper.",
      "image": "https://www.seriouseats.com/thmb/ZgG_WUA_bQEmLhOQ9OaMUo2mfnA=/1500x0/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc()/20230714-SEA-BucatiniallAmatriciana-MaureenCelestine007-29ae20e2c2fc4a2da936c0b8285311bf.jpg",
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Meanwhile, boil pasta in salted water until just shy of al dente, about 1 minute less than package recommends. Using tongs, transfer pasta to sauce, along with 1/4 cup pasta cooking water. Cook over high heat, stirring and tossing rapidly, until pasta is al dente and sauce has thickened and begins to coat noodles. Remove from heat, add cheese, and stir rapidly to incorporate. Season to taste with more salt and pepper. Serve right away, passing more cheese at the table.",

  "review": [
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Cristiana"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Didn't this recipe used to have thinly sliced onions? Maybe I'm confusing it with something else, but I could swear I've made this recipe multiple times. It's the only amatriciana in my bookmarks. I feel like I'm going crazy lol"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Ananonnie"
      },
      "reviewBody": "I made this with the stated amount of tomato and I thought it was plenty saucy, but I did use crushed tomatoes to ensure I'd get well-coated pasta. I think depending on your canned tomatoes you can end up with a different result. Some whole canned tomatoes feel really firm and if you crush them by hand, they just don't make for a very saucy end result. I like either Cento or imported San Marzano tomatoes for this reason\u2014the tomatoes are soft. \n\nI didn't feel like going to Manhattan for guanciale, so I went to Muncan, where I was told by them that they sometimes make guanciale. I got there and they didn't have any and steered me toward some Slana, which is a cured fatback they make, and obviously is even fattier than guanciale. So when I made this I drained the fat then added some back and continued with the wine. I added some more fat to taste to the sauce. The fatback did taste a lot like guanciale, and a bonus is that it's cheaper, too."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Randall Wilkins"
      },
      "reviewBody": "A few comments. I think the ratio of pork to tomato is off and inauthentic. It feels Italian - American with all that tomato. I would recommend 14 ounces or 400 mg of tomatoes to 4 to 6 ounces or 150 mg of pork. Also Pecorino Romano ( the usual kind found in the U.S. ) is saltier than Pecorino Amatrician. The best solution is half Pecorino Romano and half Parmesan Reggiano . Finally , the pork is usually removed after deglazing and then the tomatoes are added. It allows one to further crush the tomatoes more easily with a wooden spoon or potato masher like Kenji would use."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "reviewRating": {
        "@type": "Rating",
        "ratingValue": "5"
      },
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "shinyfirefly"
      },
      "reviewBody": "I saw this dish for the first time recently prepared by Top Chef contestant Buddha Lo (he won that week with it) and it was so simple and fresh looking, I had to try it. I looked at dozens of recipes for this dish, old and new, including the original recipe by traditionalist chefs Giuliano Bugialli and Marcella Hazan's preparation (who insists on butter in the sauce with no mention of guinacale). I made my own judgements regarding these adaptations, plus the onion and garlic, and opted to leave all those extras out. I wanted to experience the true flavor combination designed to honor the dish. I'm glad I did! My preparation resembles yours and like you ,I found it complex in its simplicity. I did decide to use pancetta since the guincale at my local grocer appeared dull and was pre-diced. I also increased the amount to 10 oz. so I'd have some crispy bits on top. I used a dry Frascati wine, which hails from the Lazio region near Rome. I pureed my San Marzano tomatoes, which is the preference of my husband and didn't miss the texture of hand crushed. Happy to say I'll be making this regularly from now on. Now...on to master Carbonara!"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Carter B"
      },
      "reviewBody": "I finally made this last night. I didn't have the chance to get to a store which might have guanciale or even pancetta that wasn't already thinly sliced, so I just used some \"salt pork\" cured pork belly. It was still delicious! I'll probably go for a larger pinch of red pepper flakes next time as it wasn't noticeably spicy."
    }

        "name": "Tagore Smith"
      },
      "reviewBody": "This is indeed a crowd-pleaser. \n\nActually, a few years go my mother died of cancer, and one of her closest friends died of stomach cancer a couple of months later. He stopped eating a while before he died, partially because people kept trying to feed him his favorite dishes from his childhood in Germany- why they thought he would be able to eat schnitzel is a bit beyond me.\n\nSo I made a big vat of broth and took it to him. It was not much in the way of nourishment, but it was something, and he could drink it.\n\nHis whole family had arrived, and what I knew from my mother's death was that about the only thing you can really do for someone's family when they are dying is make sure they don't have to worry about how they're going to eat. Condolences are nice, but dinner is better (and thanks to everyone in Texas who fed me during that time.) So on top of the vat of broth I made for him I made several batches of cacciatore for his family and brought them by.\n\nA while later his partner got in touch with me and asked: \"Could you come over some time and make that? It was amazing.\" So we had a couple of people round and had a nice dinner in memory of our friend.\n\nNow, you might find that story a bit ghoulish- I don't. I think it's a testament to the power of food. When you're sitting at a deathbed it's hard to think about anything else, and it's very hard to enjoy anything. If a cacciatore can give you a bit of pleasure, well, it has done its job."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Jonnyjambalaya"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Tagore Smith, not ghoulish at all. I've been through this and you got it exactly right."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Tagore Smith"
      },
      "reviewBody": "I first learned to make Cacciatore from Marcella Hazan's book, but I modified it a bit as time went on. This recipe is close to what I settled on, though I continue to include carrot and celery (which I think work well in Cacciatore- the carrot in particular adds a sweet note that I like.) And I do it on the stovetop. I guess I'll stop feeling like a heretic for using red bell pepper and not flouring the chicken.   "recipeIngredient": [
    "4  guajillo peppers (seeds removed.)",
    "4  ancho peppers (seeds removed.)",
    "2  garlic cloves chopped",
    "1/4 teaspoon Mexican oregano",

  "recipeInstructions": [
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 1,
      "name": "",
      "text": "Let's start first with the enchilada sauce. Slightly roast the peppers in a hot griddle, pressing them flat with the help of a spatula. Make sure NOT to burn them. This step takes a few seconds on each side of the peppers.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": "",
      "text": "Once roasted, place them in a saucepan with water and turn the heat to medium and simmer for about 15 minutes or when they look soft.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": "",
      "text": "Remove saucepan from stove and let them cool for another 10-15 minutes. The pepper skins should look soft.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": "",
      "text": "After the resting period, drain the peppers and place in the blender along with the garlic cloves. Add 1/2 cup of clean water and blend until you have a smooth sauce. If necessary, strain the sauce into a large bowl using a fine strainer. Season with the oregano, salt, and pepper, and set aside.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 5,
      "name": "",
      "text": "Preheat your oven to 350 degrees, just to keep the red enchiladas warm while you finish assembling them. Add the 2 tablespoons of vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add oil little by little as needed. To much oil will get a soggy tortilla.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 6,
      "name": "",
      "text": "Dip the tortilla into the enchilada sauce to lightly coat each side.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 7,
      "name": "",
      "text": "Place it in the Frying Comal-pan  or skillet and briefly fry a few seconds on both sides. Add more vegetable oil to the skillet as needed.  Place fried tortillas in a dish while you make the rest of the tortillas to keep warm in the oven.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 8,
      "name": "",
      "text": "To assemble the red enchiladas, first, place the filling in the center of the tortilla and fold it. Sometimes I place a meat filling into the center of the tortilla and then roll it, like in the pictures above.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null

  "recipeInstructions": [
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 1,
      "name": "Make the croutons",
      "text": "Heat the olive oil over medium heat in a large frying pan. Add the garlic and saute for 1 minute. Remove from the heat and let stand for 10 minutes to infuse the garlic flavor into the oil. Remove the garlic pieces and discard. Return the pan to medium heat. Add the bread cubes and saute, stirring frequently, until lightly browned, 3 to 5 minutes. Transfer to a small bowl and set aside.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": "Cook the beans",
      "text": "Combine in a soup pot the white beans, water, 1/4 teaspoon of the salt and the bay leaf. Bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to low, cover partially and simmer until the beans are tender, 60 to 75 minutes. Drain the beans, reserving 1/2 cup of the cooking liquid. Discard the bay leaf. Place the cooked beans into a large bowl and save the cooking pot for later use.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": "Make bean paste",
      "text": "In a small bowl, combine the reserved cooking liquid and 1/2 cup of the cooked beans. Mash with a fork to form a paste. Stir the bean paste into the cooked beans.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": "Saut\u00e9 vegetables",
      "text": "Return the cooking pot to the stovetop and add the olive oil. Heat over medium-high heat. Stir in the onion and carrots and saute until the carrots are tender-crisp, 6 to 7 minutes. Stir in the garlic and cook until softened, about 1 minute.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 5,
      "name": "Finish the stew",
      "text": "Stir in the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt, the pepper, chopped rosemary, bean mixture and stock. Bring to a boil then reduce the heat to low and simmer until the stew is heated through, about 5 minutes.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 6,
      "name": "Serve",
      "text": "Ladle the stew into warmed bowls and sprinkle with the croutons. Garnish each bowl with a rosemary sprig and serve immediately.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    }
  ],
  "notes": "This stew uses cannellini, a type of white bean often used in soups and stews in Tuscany. Serve it as a main course with a simple salad of mixed greens.   "recipeIngredient": [

    "300 g waxy potatoes (eg. Maris Peer/Charlotte/Jersey Royals \u2013 peeled and diced (or sliced into finger nail-sized pieces))",

    "1 tsp fine sea salt",

    "110 g lard (or Trex white vegetable fat)  (very cold and cubed)",
    "2 large eggs (UK large (Canadian \u2018Extra Large\u2019; Australian \u2018Jumbo\u2019; and US \u2018Extra or Very Large\u2019))",
    "5 tbsp very cold water",
    "extra flour for dusting and rolling (I use GFA Blend B)",
    "an additional egg and a drop of milk (beaten together)"

  "recipeInstructions": [
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 1,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Toss pine nuts with 1 teaspoon olive oil and transfer to a large plate. Toast by microwaving on high power for 2 minutes. Continue microwaving at 30-second intervals until golden brown and nutty, 3 to 8 minutes total. Alternatively, toast in a toaster oven set at 375\u00b0F (190\u00b0C) until golden brown and nutty, about 15 minutes. Set aside.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 2,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Heat 4 tablespoons oil in a large non-stick or cast iron skillet over high heat until shimmering. Add eggplant and cook, tossing occasionally, until completely softened and browned in spots (eggplant will initially absorb all of the oil then slowly release some of it), about 6 minutes.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 3,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Push eggplant to the side of the skillet and add 2 more tablespoons oil to the center. Add scallions, celery, bell pepper, and garlic and toss to combine with the eggplant. Cook, stirring and tossing frequently, until vegetables are softened and aromatic, about 3 minutes longer.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 4,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Add reserved pine nuts, mint, parsley, tomato paste, ground cinnamon, raisins, capers, sugar, red wine vinegar, and balsamic vinegar and toss to combine. Drizzle in remaining olive oil and bring to a simmer, adding water a tablespoon at a time as necessary until caponata has a sauce-like consistency that is loose, but doesn't run freely over a plate. Season to taste with salt and pepper.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    },
    {
      "@type": "HowToStep",
      "position": 5,
      "name": null,
      "text": "Let mixture cool to room temperature or refrigerate in a sealed container for up to a week. Serve at room temperature garnished with extra mint leaves and a drizzle of olive oil if desired. Serve with toasted bread or pasta.",
      "image": null,
      "imageCredit": null
    }
  ],

    {
      "@type": "Review",

      },
      "reviewBody": "I would like to make this ahead for a party. Can it be frozen?"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "GarrickWinter"
      },
      "reviewBody": "Tried this and it was amazingly good!\n\nI varied it up slightly - replaced the sugar with about half as much honey, replaced the raisins with currants (I hate raisins, sorry!), and replaced the parsely and mint with fresh lemon balm from my herb garden. Also had to use the smaller lemon-sized eggplants instead of the large ones because that's all the grocery store had, but it didn't seem to matter. One of the best meals I've had in a while!\n\nI did encounter an interesting choice in the supermarket - there were two kinds of capers, the little round ones and larger, (US) football-shaped ones about 1-2 cm long. I gather the smaller ones are immature buds and the larger ones are the mature fruit? I got the larger ones and they worked great, but I'm not sure how different they are and when to use which, since I rarely buy capers anyway."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "JagdFlanker"
      },
      "reviewBody": "I'm surprised you don't caramelize the tomato paste in step 3 'with-but-separately' in the same pan as the veggies"
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "Martini1"
      },
      "reviewBody": "In the time since this recipe was published, the price of Italian pine nuts has soared. A cup of pine nuts (not the Chinese type) would cost about $35.00 in New York City. There has been some kind of disease afflicting pine trees and the availability has been severely reduced."
    },
    {
      "@type": "Review",

      },
      "reviewBody": "Made this second time tonight. Absolutely phenomenal. Will continue to make again and again."
    }
  ],
